title: History and Appreciation of Art (3000 BC to 600 AD)
summary: From the Indus Valley Civilization (2500 BC–1750 BC) to the Mauryan dynasty (3rd century BC) art and crafts developed gradually. Harappan artists were very skilled. The Mauryan period was a new beginning; the highly polished Ashokan pillars are treasures of Indian art, alongside a tradition of folk art such as crude mother-goddess figures. The Sungas continued artistic activity (the great stupa and sculptures of Sanchi in Madhya Pradesh). The Kushans, who came from outside India, helped progress and for the first time we see sculpted portraiture. The Gupta period is the golden or classical period of Indian art: refined human figures, art centres at Mathura, Sarnath, Ujjain and Ahichhatra, religious sculptures with a divine quality, the slight tilt of the lip, full roundness of figures, accurate carving and simplicity as the stylistic stamp, famous paintings of Ajanta, and cave and temple architecture (Udaygiri caves in Madhya Pradesh, and temple architecture at Nachna and Bhumara).

Medium: metal (bronze, cast). Period: Harappan, about 2500 BC. Finding site: Mohenjo-daro. Size: about 4 inches. Artist: unknown. Collection: National Museum, New Delhi. It is one of the finest examples of the artistic and technical skills of Indus Valley craftsmen and shows fine metal casting. The figure is lanky, thin and rhythmic; she is shown without clothes, with bangles from her left wrist almost to the shoulder like tribal people in Gujarat and Rajasthan today; her hair is tied in a bun, a contemporary style unlike the elaborate hair of mother-goddess figures; she stands in a resting posture with the right hand on the waist and the left hand on the left thigh. Though only about 4 inches tall it has tremendous monumentality – it seems larger.

Medium: polished sandstone. Period: Mauryan, 3rd century BC. Finding site: Rampurva. Size: about 7 ft. Collection: Indian Museum, Kolkata. Emperor Ashoka engraved his edicts and the teachings of Buddha on pillars, rocks and tablets. An Ashokan pillar has a base, a long shaft and the decorated crown called the capital; a capital usually has animal figures standing on an abacus (a thick disc) above an inverted lotus. The Bull Capital has a bell-shaped inverted lotus as base, an abacus with plant designs (motifs that came from the Middle East or post-Greek style) and a majestic bull on top. The plain bull contrasts with the ornate lotus and abacus; the part of stone between the four legs is not carved out, but this does not disturb the strength and beauty. Its extremely high polish is the main characteristic of Mauryan sculpture, a technique learnt from Middle Eastern sculptors.

Medium: wall painting (mural) in tempera, not fresco. Period: Gupta–Vakataka, 2nd century AD to 6th century AD (most Ajanta paintings were done in the Vakataka period). Finding site: Ajanta caves, near Aurangabad in Maharashtra, named after the village Ajintha. Size: about 20 ft x 6 ft. The caves, including the unfinished one, are thirty; some were chaityas (worship places) and most were viharas (monasteries). Ajanta paintings were done in two phases: Hinayana (Buddha shown in symbols) and Mahayana (Buddha in human form; the Black Princess belongs to the Mahayana phase). The themes are mainly religious but the paintings can be enjoyed by common people. The free-flowing line, subtle rhythm of the body contour, slight tilt of the face and curves of the eyes show the artist's mastery; the colours are earthly and not loud; there is a lyrical quality and a heavenly softness in the bending of the neck. The depiction of women is the pinnacle of Ajanta.

vsa: Describe the Dancing Girl and mention its finding site.

The Dancing Girl is a metal statue of about 4 inches height from the Harappan period (2500 BC), found at Mohenjo-daro and now in the National Museum, New Delhi. The figure is lanky, thin and rhythmic, without clothes, with bangles on the left arm and hair tied in a bun; she stands in a resting posture with her right hand at the waist. It shows fine metal casting.

sa: Give a description of the works of the Indus Valley Civilization.

The Indus Valley (Harappan) Civilization flourished between 2500 and 1750 BC with main sites at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa. Great numbers of art objects and antiquities have been found: seals, pottery, jewellery, tools, toys, statuettes and utilitarian objects. The Dancing Girl in metal shows fine casting and a rhythmic figure; mother-goddess figures in crude folk style were also made.
'Black Princess' is no doubt one of the best examples of Ajanta painting. Why?

The free-flowing line, the subtle rhythm of the body contour, the slight tilt of the face and the curves of the eyes show the artist's control over the brush. Even the damaged painting shows how beautiful the colours were; they are earthy and soft, and there is a lyrical, heavenly quality in the softness of the contour and the bending of the neck.
Why is the Gupta period called the golden or classical period of Indian art?

Refinement came in the human figure; sculptures show a perfect balance of style, skill and imagination, and religious sculptures have a divine quality; the stylistic stamp was the slight tilt of the lip, roundness of the figures, accurate carving and simplicity; secular sculpture was also produced; Ajanta paintings and cave and temple architecture developed; and arts and sciences all progressed.

The Mauryan period (3rd century BC) was a new beginning. Ashoka erected pillars with edicts and Buddha's teachings in almost every region of India; each pillar has a base, shaft and capital with animal figures on an abacus above an inverted lotus. The sculptures are extremely polished and show mastery in carving animals, as in the Rampurva Bull Capital in polished sandstone.
la: Describe the Dancing Girl of the Indus Valley and its characteristics.

The Dancing Girl (metal, Harappan period, 2500 BC, Mohenjo-daro, about 4 inches, National Museum, New Delhi) is one of the finest examples of Indus Valley metal casting. The figure is lanky, thin and rhythmic. She is shown without clothes, with bangles from her wrist almost to the shoulder of her left arm, like tribal people of Gujarat and Rajasthan today. Her hair is tied in a bun, a contemporary style. She stands in a resting posture with the right hand at her waist and the left hand on her left thigh. The casting is perfect, and the little statue has great monumentality.
Explain the Rampurva Bull Capital as a work of Mauryan art.

It is a polished sandstone Ashokan capital of about 7 ft from Rampurva, now in the Indian Museum, Kolkata. It has a bell-shaped inverted lotus as base, an abacus with plant motifs and a majestic bull on top. The bull dominates the ornate lotus and abacus; the weight and power of the animal are felt and the unfinished stone between the legs does not disturb its beauty. The extremely high polish, learnt from Middle Eastern sculptors, is a main characteristic of Mauryan sculpture.
Write an appreciation of the Ajanta painting 'Black Princess'.

The Black Princess is a Gupta–Vakataka mural (about 20 ft x 6 ft) in tempera from the Mahayana phase at Ajanta. The free-flowing line, subtle rhythm of the body contour, slight tilt of the face and curves of the eyes show the artist's mastery. Even the damaged painting shows the beauty of the colours, which are earthy and quiet. The softness of the contour and the subtle bending of the neck give it a heavenly, lyrical quality.
